big: A scheme paid its first members 10% a month. They told their friends and brought in more money. For a year, everyone was happy. Then fewer people joined, and the payments stopped overnight.

h: Where does the profit come from?
lines: My cousin got paid every month for six months. Is that not proof?
Ask where the money comes from. If it comes from new members and not from real business, the scheme must collapse when new money slows.

alt: Bars showing a scheme where promises grow faster than new money coming in
caps: Early on, new money easily covers what is promised.
By month six, promises have grown close to the new money.
By month twelve, fewer people join, and promises are bigger.
The gap cannot be covered, so the payments stop. This is a Ponzi scheme.

rows: Old members are paid from the money of new members
A group hypes a stock, then sells to those who follow
Shows made-up profit, then blocks the withdrawal
A fake official threatens you and demands money
note: No genuine officer demands payment on a phone call or video call, and none puts people under 'digital arrest'.

q: A scheme pays old members with money from new members. What is it called?
why: A mutual fund invests in a portfolio of securities, under strict regulation.
Paying old members from new members' money is the mark of a Ponzi scheme.
A fixed deposit earns interest from the bank's lending business.
A bond is a loan that the issuer repays from its own business.

q: A group urges members to buy a little-known stock today, before 'the big jump'. What may be going on?
opts: A safe tip from some honest experts
A government plan to lift the stock price
A rule that the stock must rise
A pump and dump, to sell to followers
why: Honest experts do not rush strangers into little-known stocks.
Government plans are not announced in private chat groups.
No rule makes a stock rise, so this claim is false.
A group can hype a stock, push the price up and then sell to those who follow.

q: Rohan's trading app shows growing profit, but blocks his withdrawal and asks for more money first. What is likely?
opts: A way to cut his tax
why: Made-up profits and blocked withdrawals are the mark of a fake app.
Real platforms process withdrawals without asking for more deposits.
Tax has nothing to do with a blocked withdrawal.
A genuine bonus does not come with a demand for more money.

q: A caller says he is an officer and demands money to avoid arrest. What should Meena do?
opts: Pay quickly to avoid any trouble
Stay on the video call as he asks her
Hang up and report it as a fraud
Share her bank details to prove who she is
why: Paying only feeds the fraud, and the demands will grow.
Staying on the line gives the fraudster more time to pressure her.
No genuine officer demands payment over the phone, so she should report it.
Her bank details would help the fraudster take money from her.

pts: A Ponzi scheme pays old members from new members' money, and collapses.
Made-up profits and blocked withdrawals are a fake app's mark.
No real officer demands money over a call.
